prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

The days are dog-eared, the edges torn, ragged—like those pages I ripped once out of library books, for their photos of Vallejo and bootless Robert Johnson. A fine needs paying now it’s true, but not by me. I am no more guilty than that thrush is who sits there stripping moss off the wet bark of a tree. A red fleck, like his, glows at the back of my head—a beauty mark, left by the brain’s after-jets. I would not wish for the three brains Robert required to double-clutch his guitar and chase those sounds he had to know led down and into a troubled dusky river, always. Three brains did Johnson no earthly good, neither his nor Vallejo’s 4 & 1/2 worked right exactly—O bunglers, O banged-up pans of disaster! Crying for days, said Cesar, & singing for months. How can I be so strong some times, at others weak? I wish to be free, but free to do what? To leave myself behind? To switch channels remotely? Better to sing. Not like the bird, but as they sang, Cesar & Robert— with the shocked & seeded sweetness of an apple split open by a meat cleaver.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: The, Vallejo, Robert

outputs.L1:
The days are dog-eared, their edges torn and ragged—like the pages I once ripped from library books for their photographs of Vallejo and bootless Robert Johnson. A fine must be paid now, it is true, but not by me. I am no more guilty than the thrush perched there, stripping moss from the wet bark of a tree. A red fleck, like his, glows at the back of my head—a beauty mark left by the brain’s after-jets.

I would not wish for the three brains Robert required to double-clutch his guitar and pursue those sounds he must have known led, always, down and into a troubled, dusky river. Three brains did Johnson no earthly good; neither his nor Vallejo’s four and a half worked quite right—O bunglers, O battered pans of disaster! Crying for days, said Cesar, and singing for months.

How can I be so strong at times, and at others so weak? I wish to be free, but free to do what? To leave myself behind? To switch channels remotely? Better to sing—not like the bird, but as Cesar and Robert sang: with the shocked and seeded sweetness of an apple split open by a meat cleaver.
outputs.L2: The days look worn from handling, their corners frayed and shredded, like the photographs of Vallejo and shoeless Robert Johnson I once tore from library books. Yes, there is a penalty due now, but I am not the one who should pay it. I bear no more blame than the thrush perched over there, peeling moss from the rain-dark trunk of a tree. At the rear of my skull, a small red spark like the bird’s shines—a kind of birthmark of beauty, left behind by the brain’s fading exhaust. I would never ask for the three brains Robert needed in order to work his guitar’s double clutch and pursue those notes he must have understood would always carry him downward, inward, toward a troubled twilight river. Johnson’s three brains did him no good in this world; nor did Vallejo’s four and a half function quite as they should—oh clumsy wrecks, oh dented vessels of calamity! César spoke of weeping for days and singing for months. Why is it that I can be powerful at certain moments and helpless at others? I want freedom, but freedom for what purpose? To abandon who I am? To change the station from a distance? It is better to sing. Not the way a bird sings, but the way César and Robert sang—with the startled, seed-filled sweetness of an apple split apart by a butcher’s cleaver.
outputs.L3:
The speaker begins by comparing their damaged days to pages torn from library books. This image suggests a life marked by loss, interruption, and missing pieces—days that should have formed a complete record but have instead been ripped away. The mention of an unpaid library fine adds another layer to the image: the speaker is being charged for damage, as if they are responsible for the ruin. However, they refuse to accept this fine as proof of their guilt. In other words, they reject the idea that their suffering, brokenness, or past damage is entirely their own fault.

The speaker then presents themselves as innocent, comparing their actions to those of a thrush stripping moss from wet bark. This natural image emphasizes instinct rather than wrongdoing. The bird is not acting out of malice; it is simply doing what it does to survive. By identifying with the thrush, the speaker suggests that their own behavior may also come from necessity, vulnerability, or instinct rather than moral failure.

The poem then connects the speaker’s troubled mind and suffering to two important artistic figures: Robert Johnson and César Vallejo. Johnson, the legendary blues musician, and Vallejo, the Peruvian poet, are portrayed as gifted but deeply wounded individuals. Both transformed pain into art. By placing themselves alongside Johnson and Vallejo, the speaker frames suffering not only as damage but also as a source of song, poetry, and vision. Their pain becomes part of a larger tradition of artists who carried private wounds and turned them into powerful expression.

The speaker also questions their own changing nature, especially the way they move between strength and weakness. At times, they may feel resilient, capable, or defiant; at other times, they feel broken or overwhelmed. This uncertainty leads them to ask what true freedom would actually mean. Is freedom the ability to escape pain? Is it freedom from guilt, from memory, from the self? Or is it something more complicated: the ability to live honestly within one’s own damaged life?

By the end, the speaker seems to decide that singing is better than trying to escape the self. Like Robert Johnson and César Vallejo, they recognize that art may not remove suffering, but it can give suffering a form and a voice. Singing becomes an act of survival, not denial. Rather than fleeing from who they are, the speaker chooses expression, suggesting that true freedom may lie not in escape, but in transforming pain into song.
outputs.L4:
I think of guilt as a room with no door, only windows painted shut. Inside it, the torn pages of books drift across the floor like feathers, each one carrying a sentence I once refused to finish. Some are stained with rain, some with wine, some with the fingerprints of whoever tried to save them before giving up. I gather them in my hands and cannot put them back in order. The book is damaged, but it still speaks. Its ruined spine still remembers the shape of a song.

There are birds in the rafters, restless and dark. They beat their wings against the ceiling as if the sky were only one more thing denied to them. I envy them their panic, their honest desire to escape. Even when they fail, they fail upward. Even when they are trapped, they keep making the motion of freedom.

I think of César Vallejo, who knew how sorrow could enter the body like bread, ordinary and necessary. I think of him writing from the wound, from exile, from poverty, from the bewildered human heart that asks forgiveness before it knows its crime. His sadness was not clean. It was not beautiful in the easy way. It limped. It stuttered. It carried the weight of all the broken men walking home at dusk with nothing in their pockets but hunger and a little stubborn light.

And I think of Robert Johnson at the crossroads, his guitar held like a confession. Whether or not the devil came is almost beside the point. Everyone who has suffered knows the bargain already: to be given a voice, you must first be hollowed out enough for something to pass through you. The strings do not sing because they are whole. They sing because they are tightened, struck, made to tremble.

Genius, if it comes, comes damaged. It arrives with torn sleeves, with mud on its shoes, with a mouth full of ash. It does not excuse the harm we have done or the harm done to us. It does not make guilt disappear. It only gives the guilt a rhythm, a pulse, a way to move through the body without becoming a grave.

So I do not believe anymore in perfect freedom. The birds are always partly caged. The book is always partly ruined. The poet is always speaking from some fracture in the soul, and the bluesman is always bending the note because the straight note cannot hold the truth.

But there is another kind of release. Not escape, exactly. Transformation. The page torn from the book becomes a wing. The wound becomes a mouth. The burden becomes music. What cannot be forgiven may still be sung. What cannot be repaired may still be shaped into something fierce and necessary.

And perhaps that is beauty: not purity, not peace, not the absence of pain, but the raw sound made when suffering refuses to remain silent.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dense, surreal prose poem in the voice of a guilty but defiant speaker, weaving together references to César Vallejo, Robert Johnson, library books, birds, brains, freedom, and singing.
counterfactuals.output:
I returned the library books late, yes, with rain in their lungs and my fingerprints blooming like small dark verdicts on the margins; charge me the fine, nail the notice to my door, I have already paid in feathers, in sleepless hemispheres of brain, in the blue coins of every song I swallowed and could not keep. César Vallejo sat in the corner of the reading room with Wednesday broken across his knees, saying there are blows in life and also overdue stamps, and I said brother, I know, I have struck myself against the catalog and come away alphabetized by sorrow. Down at the crossroads, Robert Johnson tuned a guitar with strings made from the nerves of migratory birds, and every note flew out crooked, guilty, free—free the way a cage remembers the hand that opened it and hates the hand for being necessary.

Do not ask me to confess neatly. My brain is a burned-out aviary, full of beaks tapping equations into the skull, full of sparrows wearing judges’ wigs, full of blackbirds rehearsing my defense in a language made of smoke. I stole nothing except a little music from the mouth of suffering, a little bread from the table of silence, a few bright pages from the impossible book where the dead keep signing their names. If I sang, it was because the rope was listening. If I lied, it was because truth came limping toward me with Vallejo’s shoes and Johnson’s shadow and all the birds of the county stitched into its coat.

Yes, I am guilty: of wanting the sky without permission, of opening my head like a prohibited volume, of teaching the caged throat to counterfeit thunder. But I am defiant too, my judges, my librarians, my beautiful accusers with ink on your wings. I will stand here under the fluorescent moon, humming through the bars of my teeth, while the books rise from their shelves and beat upward, while the brains of the world unfold like wet maps, while every borrowed word becomes a bird, and every bird, escaping, sings my name incorrectly—and therefore saves me.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a lyrical paragraph in a contemporary American poetry style, with ragged imagery, blues mythology, Vallejo, Robert Johnson, a thrush on wet bark, and the line “I wish to be free, but free to do what?”
counterfactuals.output: At the crossroads, the rain keeps its own counsel, blue as a bruise under the tongue, and Robert Johnson leans into the static with a guitar full of grave-dirt and lightning; somewhere Vallejo is breaking bread with the broken, saying brother, saying bone, saying the day is a dog with wet eyes. A thrush clings to the wet bark like a brown prayer the storm forgot to finish, its throat a small torn church of music, while the city drags its chains through the gutter and calls it morning. I put my hand in my pocket and find only lint, a matchbook, a map to a house that burned down before I was born. “I wish to be free, but free to do what?” Free to howl at the moon’s bad nickel, free to love the wound without becoming it, free to walk past the devil’s booth and still hear my name tuned low in the strings.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a prose poem that feels fragmented, confessional, and intellectually haunted, comparing damaged days to torn book pages and ending with a startling image of an apple split open by a meat cleaver.
counterfactuals.output:
Some days arrive already damaged, torn loose from whatever book was trying to make a life of me. Their edges feather in my hands. A sentence begins, then disappears into pulp. I keep thinking I can smooth them flat, press them under the weight of other people’s names, but the creases remember me.

I confess: I have mistaken ruin for evidence. I have held each spoiled morning up to the light as if it were a manuscript, as if the holes might spell a doctrine. There are philosophies that sound like rooms with no doors. There are prayers that return with my own mouth inside them.

The days accumulate in a drawer: margins scribbled with hunger, paragraphs drowned in coffee, whole afternoons ripped through the spine. I read them anyway. I read what is missing. I read the ghost of the hand that tore them.

And still the mind goes on sharpening itself against what it cannot explain.

At dusk, on the table, silence gleams—an apple split open by a meat cleaver.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Imitate the style of an experimental poet: write a single paragraph meditating on guilt, beauty, music, and brokenness, mentioning César Vallejo and Robert Johnson without explaining who they are.
counterfactuals.output: Guilt enters first as a cracked bell, then beauty follows barefoot through the glass, humming what the wound cannot translate; somewhere César Vallejo folds a night into his coat, somewhere Robert Johnson bends a blue note until it limps like a saint, and I stand between them with my pockets full of broken mirrors, listening for the music that leaks from damage—not forgiveness, no, not yet, but the bright animal of it, the terrible shine, the way a ruined chord can still open its mouth and become a room, the way every fracture learns to sing by refusing to close.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a strange literary monologue about stolen library pages, unpaid fines, a bird stripping moss, the mythic brains of Robert Johnson and Vallejo, and the desire to sing rather than escape.
counterfactuals.output:
I confess: it was I who stole the pages from the library.

Not whole books—never whole books. I was not greedy in the ordinary way. I took only the necessary leaves, the ones that loosened when touched, the ones already whispering themselves out of the spine. A page of astronomy with the moon gnawed into phases. A page from a grammar book explaining the future tense as if it were a hallway with clean windows. Three pages from a biography of a saint who ate only ash and figs. A map of rivers. An index. Half a poem.

The librarian knew. Of course she knew. Librarians are trained by silence to hear damage happening in other rooms. She would look at me over her little rampart of stamped cards and say nothing, only tap the ledger where my unpaid fines accumulated like a second weather. I owed for late returns, for missing pages, for the book on birds I never brought back because a bird had chosen it.

That is true. A bird came to my window—small, gray, brisk with appetite—and began stripping moss from the sill. It worried the green felt loose with its beak, pulling strand after strand as if unmaking a miniature forest. I watched it labor, savage and practical, and thought: here is scholarship. Here is criticism. Here is a creature reducing the world to bedding.

Behind me lay the stolen pages, spread on the floor like the shed skins of angels. I had arranged them in circles, trying to build a brain large enough to think my way out. Not my own brain, no. Mine was a room with one chair and a single bulb trembling. I wanted the mythic brains: Robert Johnson’s, smoking at the crossroads, tuned to blue lightning and bargain-ink; Vallejo’s, bruised and planetary, full of bread, prison, rain, and the sorrow of Thursdays. I imagined their skulls as dark fruit split open, each seed a song, each wrinkle a road nobody survived unchanged.

But I did not want escape. That is the secret I have been fined for most heavily.

Everyone assumed I was tearing pages out to make a door. A paper door, a door of maps, a door of stolen sentences. They thought I wanted to flee the stacks, the city, the debt, the librarian’s mute arithmetic, the bird dismantling the moss until the window looked naked and accused.

No. I wanted to sing.

There is a difference. Escape is a mouth running away from its own hunger. Song is hunger standing still and giving itself a name.

I wanted to sing with the torn page in my hand, with the fine notice folded in my shoe, with the moss-thief bird hammering its nest together somewhere under the eaves. I wanted to sing like a man who has swallowed a library and now hears the books knocking against his ribs. Like Johnson with the devil’s receipt tucked in his hatband. Like Vallejo waking in Paris and discovering that grief had put on his coat and gone out ahead of him.

So charge me. Stamp me overdue. Write my name in the black ledger until it grows antlers. I have stolen only what was already leaving. I have paid nothing because money is the least convincing form of apology. The pages are gone, yes, but listen: in their absence the books breathe harder.

And if the librarian comes for me at last, holding the bill with both hands like a verdict, I will not climb through the window. I will not follow the bird into its hidden architecture. I will stand among the mutilated shelves, open my mouth, and make my debt audible.

Not to be forgiven.

To be heard.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
